title: Anchor — Spring 2026
coverLines: Thirteen weeks of steady, not striving
You are not holding it alone
summary: Spring 2026 study guide for Anchor (single parents): thirteen weeks of holding steady on hard water — refuge, identity, daily bread, the raising, rest, the village, provision, forgiveness, hope, co-parenting, worship, light and a future — a verse and a daily read for every day of the season.

blocks.text: How to use this study guide

This is a study guide for Anchor. Somebody has to hold it all together — the school runs, the rent, the homework, the hard days, the dreams — and that somebody is you. Spring has thirteen weeks, and each week we anchor one truth under a different wave: who you are, what is enough for today, how to rest without guilt, where your village is, and what hope is doing in the kids. Each day has a verse, a few lines, one small Try it step, and a prayer. Day 5 is a short quiz; days 6 and 7 are rest and reflection days.
You are not the sea

Single parenting can feel like treading water in open ocean — every responsibility yours, every current against you. But the Anchor's whole story is that you are not the sea. You are a boat with an anchor, and the anchor is God. The name 'Anchor' isn't pressure; it's a promise: hope as an anchor for the soul, sure and firm (Hebrews 6:19). This season we practice being the boat, letting Him be the seabed.

Read the verse, read the lines, do the Try it, say the prayer. On day 5 there's a quiz; days 6 and 7 are for rest. Holding steady is not the same as holding everything. By winter you'll feel the difference.

intro.text: Before any strategy, before one more tip on parenting or money, a single parent needs to know where to run when the waves rise. This week is about the place of safety that actually holds: God as refuge and strength.

verse.text: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble.

blocks.text: The psalmist doesn't say God sends trouble or explains it. He says God is the refuge and the strength — an ever-present help in trouble, not after it. For the single parent, the storm is rarely optional: the Accent on rent, the child's grief, the unpaid bill, the loneliness. The verse's comfort is not that storms stop but that inside them there is a strong place to stand.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name today's storm honestly — don't minimize it
Put yourself inside the refuge for five minutes
Say: 'God is my ever-present help, even in this'

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be my refuge before the storm ends, not just after
Be the strength when I run out of mine

verse.text: Whoever dwells in the shelter of the Most High will rest in the shadow of the Almighty.

blocks.text: Notice the resting place: the shadow of the Almighty. A shadow means the sun is behind Him — you're standing close enough that He takes the heat. Dwell in the shelter, and the shadow becomes home. The verse promises not that no heat falls on the day, but that there is shade that holds. Get close to God today, and let Him take the burning for you.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Pull close enough to stand in His shadow
Let God take the heat of one thing today
Rest — dwelling, not just visiting

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let me dwell, not just visit, under Your shelter
Take the heat of what's crushing me today

verse.text: He stilled the storm to a whisper; the waves of the sea were hushed.

blocks.text: This psalm says the very storms HE stilled. Storms have an end because they answer to a Lord. The picture is tender: he hushes waves to a whisper. Whatever is loud in your house right now — conflict, fear, a child's screaming heart — God can bring it to a whisper. Not necessarily remove it: hush it enough for you to breathe.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Ask God to hush one loud thing today
Breathe in the whisper when He quiets it
Trust that storms end under His hand

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Hush the loud in my life to a whisper
Still the waves that feel endless

verse.text: Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you.

blocks.text: The command is 'cast' — the word pictures a throw, not a polite hand-off. Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you. The 'because' is everything: not 'because you've earned relief' but because He cares. The cup of anxiety was never meant to be carried alone. Throw one load off today — a financial fear, a parenting fear, a loneliness — and let His care be the catching hands.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Pick the heaviest anxiety in you right now
Cast it — name it, and throw it to Him
Refuse to pick it back up today

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Catch what I cannot carry
Let me trust that You care, truly care

verse.text: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the refuge. One promise to remember: ever-present help, in the trouble. Check what you remember, then stand inside the refuge.

blocks.question: What does Psalm 46:1 call God for us?
options: Refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble
blocks.explain: 'God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble.' Close enough to be present, strong enough to hold.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Stand with us in the refuge
Be present in today's trouble

verse.text: In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me dwell in safety.

blocks.text: Rest day — and for a single parent rest often begins with the hardest verse: sleep. David could lie down and sleep not because the day was safe but because the Lord made him dwell in safety. The watchman's job is God's; the sleeper's job is to sleep. Tonight, or today if you're reading before bed, let the refuge finalize: you are not on watch alone.

blocks.prompt: What keeps you from real rest at night? What would it take to hand the watch to God and sleep?
blocks.placeholder: The thing keeping me awake is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let me lie down and sleep in peace
You alone make me dwell in safety

verse.text: Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.

blocks.text: The week closes at the invitation every single parent longs to hear: 'Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.' You qualify on both counts — weary and burdened. Jesus doesn't add a parenting course or a to-do list to the invitation. He takes the burden. Week one ends holding the one Anchor that holds you: not your grip on the boat, but His grip on you.

blocks.prompt: What burden did you bring to Jesus this week? Name the one you're still carrying that He is still inviting you to lay down.
blocks.placeholder: The burden still in my hands...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Take the burden You offered to take
Let me be weary-and-burdened and still come

intro.text: The storm and the exhaustion whisper a lie: 'You're just a struggling single parent.' This week we answer from the deeper place — who you actually are before God, called by name, redeemed, and irreplaceable to Him.

days.title: I have called you by name

verse.text: Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have summoned you by name; you are mine.

blocks.text: God speaks to a people who felt abandoned. He says: fear not, because three things are true — I have redeemed you, I have summoned you by name, and you are mine. Not 'you are a good parent' or 'you are coping' — you are redeemed and named and owned. Whatever the label the world or the court or your own harsh voice uses, God's version of your name comes first.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Say your own name in God's sentence: '[name], you are Mine'
Drop one label you've been answering to
Tell yourself the truth before the noise does

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Redeem me again into who I am
Let me answer to the name You call me

verse.text: So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God.

blocks.text: The fears of a single parent are specific and valid: where will the money come from? Will I do enough? What if my child goes wrong? And the answer doesn't dismiss the fear — it addresses the object of it: I am with you; I am your God. Fear shrinks when God is in the frame, not because the storm vanished, but because 'with you' outranks the storm.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name today's specific fear out loud
Follow it with: 'but I am with you,' says God
Let 'your God' do the steadying, not your plans

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be with me through the fear, not around it
Let dismay bow to 'I am your God'

verse.text: As a mother comforts her child, so will I comfort you.

blocks.text: Here God gives you the most tender name He could: He is like a mother comforting her child. The God of the universe knows the sound of a mother's comfort, because He invented it. Whatever you've lost — a partner, a parent, support, recognition — the One who mothers you has not stopped comforting you. And the comfort you pour into your children is the same comfort first poured into you.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Receive God's comfort like a child — don't resist it
Let His comfort fill you before you pour it out
Comfort a child the way you're being comforted

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Comfort me as a mother comforts a child
Let the comfort I receive become the comfort I give

verse.text: Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.

blocks.text: The world has a pattern for 'single parent' and it includes pity, guilt and less-than. Romans 12:2 is the rebellion verse: don't conform to the pattern; get transformed by a renewed mind. Your mind is renewed by truth — starting with the truth you're feeding it this week. You are not the world's pattern; you are God's dearly held name. Let the renewing begin.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Catch one 'single-parent pattern' thought today
Renew it with a verse from this week
Let transformation, not conformity, have your mind

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Renew my mind with who I am in You
Break the world's pattern off my self-image

verse.text: I have summoned you by name; you are mine.

blocks.text: Quiz day on identity. One truth to hold above the storm: redeemed, named, owned by God. Check what you remember, then walk in your real name.

blocks.question: In Isaiah 43:1, what does God say to His people who fear?
options: By name you are Mine; I have redeemed you
blocks.explain: 'I have redeemed you; I have summoned you by name; you are mine.' You are claimed by name before you do anything.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep telling me my true name
Let Your claim on me outshout the labels

verse.text: He tends his flock like a shepherd: He gathers the lambs in his arms and carries them close to his heart.

blocks.text: Rest day — and today the Shepherd's tenderness is for you too. 'He gathers the lambs in his arms' is a verse about the flock; the single parent is a lamb and a shepherd at once. You carry your children, and He carries you close to His heart. Let the carrying happen. Rest doesn't make you less of a parent; it makes you a lamb being carried.

blocks.prompt: When did you last let yourself be carried — not carrying, not coping, but carried? What would it look like this week?
blocks.placeholder: Being carried would look like...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Carry me close to Your heart today
Let me be the lamb before I am the shepherd

verse.text: I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful.

blocks.text: The week ends where identity always ends: in the Maker's workshop. You are fearfully and wonderfully made — the same hands that knit your children together stitched you too. A person this carefully made and this personally kept has a name that outlasts the hardest season. Let 'wonderfully made' finish the week. It is not arrogance; it is worship.

blocks.prompt: What in you — not in spite of your story but within it — shows the Maker's care? Sit with being wonderfully made rather than merely surviving.
blocks.placeholder: The wonderful in me is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Thank You for making me fearfully and wonderfully
Let me live from that word, not from the label

intro.text: A single parent's mind is often three months ahead — rent, school fees, emergencies. This week gets the care back down to one day at a time: God's provision is dosed daily, like manna, and that is enough.

verse.text: Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.

blocks.text: Jesus doesn't say tomorrow won't have trouble; He says today already has its share, and He will be there for it. Worry about tomorrow borrows trouble that isn't due yet and pays for it with today's peace. The single parent isn't asked to skip planning — only to stop inventing a tomorrow God hasn't given yet. Give today your attention; give the future to the Father.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Catch one 'tomorrow' worry and arrest it
Do one fully-present thing for today only
Say: 'today has enough; so does tomorrow's Grace'

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Pull my heart back into today
Let me not pay tomorrow's trouble with today's peace

verse.text: The people are to go out each day and gather enough for that day.

blocks.text: God fed Israel in the desert with daily bread — enough for that day, then more the next morning. He could have stocked a month of manna; He deliberately rationed it to daily. Not because He's stingy, but because daily dependence keeps the relationship alive. Your daily bread (rent this month, food this week) is not an accident of your income; it is a daily relationship with a Provider who wants your trust, not your hoarding.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name what 'manna for today' looks like in your house
Receive today's provision with thanks
Resist the stockpile anxiety — He's coming tomorrow too

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give me today's bread as You gave Israel manna
Let daily dependence be my daily intimacy

verse.text: See how the flowers of the field grow… If that is how God clothes the grass… will he not much more clothe you?

blocks.text: Jesus points at a flower to prove a point to worried people: God clothes grass, and you are worth more than grass. It's not a guarantee of plenty; it is a guarantee of the Gardener's care. The school uniform will be found, the cupboards will be covered, the month will be healed. Not by your calculation alone, but by a Father who clothes the lilies and counts the children's sparrows.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Look at a flower (or a photo) and say: 'He cares for me more'
Name one provision God has already made this season
Trade one anxiety for a 'lily' promise

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Clothe this family like You clothe the lilies
Let Your care for me outrun my calculation

verse.text: The jar of flour will not be used up and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the Lord sends rain on the land.

blocks.text: One widow, one jar of flour, one jug of oil — and a miracle that renewed itself daily. The story of the widow at Zarephath is your story: nearly empty, yet never empty, because the Lord kept the daily measure flowing. God's provision often looks like 'just enough, again.' Don't despise the smallness of the flowing. The widow's household ate because God sustained a barely-full jar.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Recognize your 'barely-full jar' — and that you're still eating
Thank God for the daily-flow provision
Trust the jar while it's flowing, even when it's low

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Sustain my jar until the rain comes
Turn my 'nearly empty' into 'never empty'

verse.text: Each day has enough trouble of its own.

blocks.text: Quiz day on enough. One discipline to own: live in the day God gave. Check what you remember, then put the month down and pick the day up.

blocks.question: According to Matthew 6:34, why should we not worry about tomorrow?
options: Tomorrow has enough trouble of its own
God has no plan for it
blocks.explain: 'Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.' Grace comes daily, not in advance.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Anchor me to today
Let each day's trouble meet each day's grace

verse.text: On the sixth day they gathered twice as much… and he said, 'Tomorrow is to be a day of sabbath rest.'

blocks.text: Rest day — and the manna story has rest built in: on the sixth day, twice the manna, because the seventh is rest. God rationed daily bread AND made room for a full stop. A single parent needs the sabbath stop more than most. The week's whole rhythm is proof: God orders provision AND orders rest. Let today be your seventh — pick up the bread that's already there, and don't collect on the sabbath.

blocks.prompt: What would a genuine stop look like in your week — where provision is already set aside and you're allowed to cease?
blocks.placeholder: My sabbath stop would look like...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Grant me the seventh-day stop
Show me where the bread for this rest already is

verse.text: Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground outside your Father's care. And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered.

blocks.text: The week ends with the most intimate math in Scripture: sparrows counted, and your hairs numbered. God who orders the small birds' falls also numbers the details of your head — every hair of a stressed single parent. The God of daily manna and never-runs-out oil is also the God who counts your hairs. You are not one concern among millions in His book; you are a numbered, sparrow-seen, hair-counted beloved.

blocks.prompt: What 'small thing' of your world right now can you hand to the God who counts hairs — not even too small for His care?
blocks.placeholder: I'm handing You the small thing of...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Number my cares like You number my hairs
Let me be counted, seen and provided for

weeks.title: Week 4 — The long way to the heart
weeks.theme: The long way to the heart

intro.text: The deepest anchor-work is the raising of the children — but it is long, mostly quiet, and results aren't quarterly. This week we tend the relationship that is the real curriculum: hearts, not just grades.

verse.text: Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.

blocks.text: 'The way they should go' can be read as the way their nature points — the specific shape God put in each child. Training isn't mass-producing obedience; it's finding the groove each heart was made for and aiming it Godward. You can't see the end result from here; the promise spans 'even when they are old.' You're planting for a harvest you may not witness. That's the long way, and it's worth it.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Notice one strength in your child's 'way' today
Aim it Godward with one conversation
Plant one patient seed; don't demand the fruit today

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Show me each child's unique 'way'
Let the long training yield faithful grown-ups

verse.text: Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

blocks.text: Paul's parenting verse has first a negative: don't exasperate. Don't provoke, don't set a standard they can never reach, don't make your love conditional on performance. A single parent already carries questions of 'am I enough' — the child feels it too. The instruction of the Lord only lands in unexasperated hearts. Check your pace today: is the training, or the frustration, leading?

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Notice one way you may exasperate without meaning to
Adjust the standard to the child, not the ideal
Teach one thing in the Lord's patience, not your pressure

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep my words from exasperating
Let me train in the Lord's calm, not my fuel

verse.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is… patience… against such things there is no law.

blocks.text: Parenting is the most patience-intensive job on earth, and patience is named the fruit of the Spirit — not a natural talent. The good news of the fruit list: it grows from the Spirit, not your temperament. On the days you're out of patience, the Spirit isn't out of His. Ask for long patience for the long way; the fruit is His to grow in you.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Ask the Spirit for one day's patience, not a life's
Breathe before the repeat question today
Receive fruit you can't produce — it's His

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Grow patience in me — I can't manufacture it
Let the Spirit's fruit outlast my frustration

verse.text: Children obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honor your father and mother… that it may go well with you.

blocks.text: There is a design to the home: children obey 'in the Lord,' parents train 'in the Lord.' The family follows the same shape as the gospel — grace at the top, gratitude at the bottom. When a single parent leads 'in the Lord' (not in fear, not in guilt), the children's honor has somewhere true to attach. The way it 'goes well' is the whole rhythm honoring God.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Lead one instruction 'in the Lord' — with grace on top
Explain the why, not just the no
Let honor at home echo honor to God

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give my home the gospel's shape
Turn our obedience into worship

verse.text: Start children off on the way they should go.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the raising. One promise to hold: the long way is worth planting. Check what you remember, then keep training the untrainable-seeming today.

blocks.question: What is the promise of Proverbs 22:6 about training a child?
options: Instant results if you're firm enough
Even when old, they will not turn from the way
blocks.explain: 'Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.' A long-term promise, not a daily guarantee.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Bless this long and steady raising
Let the training bear fruit they'll carry

verse.text: He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the rest, for a parent working a long harvest, is in the 'not finished yet' promise. The good work God began in you, and in your children, is being carried on to completion by the same hand. You don't see the end from here, and you don't have to. Rest in the phrase 'will carry it on.' The finishing is His department; today is yours, and today you may rest.

blocks.prompt: Which of your children needs you to trust the unfinished work most? What would resting in that look like this week?
blocks.placeholder: I can rest in the unfinished work of...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Carry on the work I cannot see finished
Let me rest in the unfinished, loved anyway

verse.text: I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, now lives in you also.

blocks.text: The week ends with Paul looking at Timothy — a young man raised by a mother and grandmother who passed sincere faith down through hard years. Lois and Eunice's story is yours: single women who gave Timothy the most lasting inheritance there is. The school fees and the discipline and the meals — all of it is scaffolding around the real thing: faith living in the next generation. You are building that. Keep the long way.

blocks.prompt: What 'sincere faith' do you want your children to say lived in you? Name one thing you're building that will outlast everything you struggle with.
blocks.placeholder: The inheritance I'm passing is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let my faith be living faith they'll inherit
Make the long way worth it — and it is

intro.text: The boat can't carry everyone if the boat is cracked. This week is about the counterintuitive act of love: caring for yourself, so you can still be there to care for them. Not luxury — stewardship.

verse.text: Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, 'Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.'

blocks.text: Jesus invited His exhausted disciples to leave the crowd and rest — note that He didn't say the crowd would stop. There will always be more need than you have strength; that's why 'come away and rest' is a command, not a suggestion. The disciples couldn't even eat. Sound familiar? A single parent eating standing up, always on. The invitation is to a quiet place. Accept it this week, even in small slices.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Schedule one quiet stretch where you can eat
Take it — the crowd will be there when you return
Stop treating rest like an indulgence

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Call me away to the quiet place
Let me rest before I break

verse.text: But those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They will soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not be faint.

blocks.text: The promise is not that strength never runs out but that it gets renewed for those who hope in the Lord. The image is as athletic as parenting: run and not grow weary, walk and not faint. Renewal is the missing discipline when single parents burn out. Hope in the Lord isn't a feeling; it's a posture — reconnecting daily to the Source of the strength you've been spending.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Hope in the Lord — renew the connection today
Do one thing that genuinely renews you (not numbs)
Spend today recognizing whose strength you're on

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Renew my strength like an eagle's
Let me walk this day and not faint

verse.text: Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up… and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed.

blocks.text: The busiest Person who ever lived protected His margin. If Jesus needed a solitary place before the day started, the single parent's need for fifteen quiet minutes is not a luxury — it's modeled by the Master. Margin is the fuel margin. Before the demands start, take the solitary place, even if it's a car parked early. The day runs differently when it first meets God.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Carve fifteen quiet minutes before the day begins
Protect them like a meeting with the Maker
Enter the day from the solitary place

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Meet me in my solitary minutes
Let the day start from the quiet, not the rush

verse.text: But he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.'

blocks.text: Paul begged for his 'thorn' to leave; God refused and gave something better — not removal but sufficiency. My grace is sufficient. For the single parent who feels the thorn of doing it alone, this is the anchor verse: God's strength is made perfect in your weakness. You are not disqualified by being worn; you are the very setting where His power shows. The cracks in the boat are where He holds.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Stop performing strength — admit the weakness
Let 'sufficient grace' settle on one area today
Brag, with Paul, about what weakness reveals

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make Your strength perfect in my weakness
Let the cracks show Your holding

verse.text: Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength.

blocks.text: Quiz day on stewarding strength. One renewal to own: hope in the Lord. Check what you remember, then take the quiet place.

blocks.question: According to Isaiah 40:31, what happens to those who hope in the Lord?
options: Their strength is renewed — they run without growing weary
blocks.explain: 'Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength… they will run and not grow weary.' Renewal, not immunity.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Renew the strength I spend on everyone
Be the fuel under my weariness

verse.text: Better one handful with tranquillity than two handfuls with toil and chasing after the wind.

blocks.text: Rest day — and this verse defends the small portion: one handful with tranquility beats two handfuls of frantic. The single parent's life often looks like two handfuls — every extra hour, every extra shift, chasing enough. Wisdom says a smaller pace that keeps your soul intact is worth more. The children would rather have a present, tranquil parent than a richer, hollow one. Eat your tranquil handful today.

blocks.prompt: Where are you chasing 'two handfuls' that costs you tranquillity? What would settling for the tranquil handful look like this week?
blocks.placeholder: The second handful I can let go of is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach me the tranquil handful
Let me choose presence over production

verse.text: But I will sing of your strength, in the morning I will sing of your love; for you are my fortress, my refuge in times of trouble.

blocks.text: The week ends looking at where the strength is held: you are my fortress, my refuge. David, exhausted by enemies, didn't end the psalm with his own stamina — he ended with God's strength, sung in the morning. The steward of strength ends where the stewarding began: not 'I am strong' but 'You are my refuge.' That's the posture that never burns out, because the fuel source never runs.

blocks.prompt: What would your week look like if you sang of His strength before your own was asked? Wake tomorrow with the fortress already in place.
blocks.placeholder: I'm learning to start with...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be my fortress before the day begins
Let me steward strength that comes from You

intro.text: The single-parent myth is that it's all on you. The Bible's story is a village: God places the lonely in families, and you were never meant to raise, provide and pray alone. This week we build the village walls.

verse.text: God sets the lonely in families.

blocks.text: One of God's specialties is settling the lonely into families — and 'family' in the Bible is bigger than blood; it's the household of faith that takes you in. The church is supposed to mother widows, father the fatherless, and widen its table for single parents. If you've been feeling profoundly alone, the first search isn't 'how do I cope alone' but 'where is the family God is setting me in?'

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Ask: where is God's family with room for me?
Reach out to one sister/brother in the church this week
Say 'help' to a family — let God set you in

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Set me in the family You've prepared
Let me receive the village without shame

verse.text: Just as a body, though one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ.

blocks.text: A body doesn't have one part do everything — eyes don't digest, hands don't see. Yet in the body of Christ, a single parent often tries to be the whole body. The invitation of the body image is division of labor: someone teaches, someone gives, someone babysits, someone prays. You are allowed to be one strong part, not all parts. Let the body help carry what the body was made to carry.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name a 'part' of the body that could hold a need
Ask that part specifically this week
Let yourself be the part you are — not all of them

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach me to be one part in a body, not a whole body
Let Your church carry in me what it was built to

verse.text: Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

blocks.text: Burden-bearing is one-way traffic; you can't carry my load while I pretend not to have one. The law of Christ is fulfilled when we let the load be shared. For the proud, independent single parent, this verse demands receiving: tell the church, tell the small group, tell one friend what's actually heavy. A burden shared is the law of Christ in motion. You fulfill it by being carried, not just by carrying.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name one burden honestly to a safe person
Ask for specific help (meals, drop-off, company)
Let the law of Christ be fulfilled through you both

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let me share my load this week
Make the burden lighter, fulfilled in Christ's law

verse.text: Whoever welcomes one of these little children in my name welcomes me; and whoever welcomes me does not welcome me but the one who sent me.

blocks.text: Jesus took a child in His arms to teach the church: count children as the measure of your welcome. A church that welcomes single parents' children is welcoming Jesus. The village is built around little ones: the teacher who notices, the family that invites your kids over, the youth leader who shows up. If your children aren't being welcomed somewhere, find the place that welcomes them — because that's where you'll both be loved.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Identify one place that genuinely welcomes your child
Let your child be 'welcomed in his name' there
Thank one volunteer who sees your kid

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Welcome my children with Jesus' welcome
Place them where they're wanted

verse.text: God sets the lonely in families.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the village. One promise to anchor: you are set in a family. Check what you remember, then go find your placement.

blocks.question: What does Psalm 68:6 say God does with the lonely?
options: Leaves them to grow strong alone
blocks.explain: 'God sets the lonely in families.' He is in the placement business — you are placed, not abandoned.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep setting me in family
Let me receive the people You place

verse.text: As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear him.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the deepest village is the Father's own compassion. Psalm 103 compares God's feeling for you to a father's — the kind of father every single parent is trying to be: compassionate, remembering you're dust, slow to anger. The village of God starts with being mothered and fathered by God Himself. Rest today in that particular tenderness. You are parented, and you are looked after.

blocks.prompt: Where do you most need God's father-mother tenderness this week? What would receiving that compassion change for you?
blocks.placeholder: I need compassion in...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Have compassion on me as a parent has on children
Be the Father-mother I and my kids need

verse.text: And in him you too are being built together to become a dwelling in which God lives by his Spirit.

blocks.text: The week closes with a beautiful turn: you and your household are being built INTO a dwelling — a place where God lives. Not a perfect house, not a two-parent ideal, but a real home where His Spirit dwells. Your family genuinely becomes a 'house of God.' The village isn't out there echoing an unemployment you lack; it's being built together, with your family as one of the living stones. Say it again: your home is a dwelling place of God.

blocks.prompt: What would change if you believed your home — exactly as it is — is a dwelling place of God by His Spirit?
blocks.placeholder: If my home is His dwelling...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Dwell in this house by Your Spirit
Make my family a living stone in Your building

intro.text: Single parent means single provider — and that can feel like feeding a family on a widening sea. This week we test the provision promises: God who has never missed a bill is not going to start missing yours.

verse.text: And my God will meet all your needs according to the riches of his glory in Christ Jesus.

blocks.text: 'All your needs' — the measure is not your income, not your network, but the riches of His glory in Christ. The verse comes after Paul thanked the Philippians for sharing in his need; it's a promise over the generosity cycle. Your needs are known, counted and met — not always in advance, not always in the shape you expected, but according to His riches, which are more than your bills.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: List one month's needs — they're already known
Put this verse next to the scariest one
Let 'His riches' out-math your shortage

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Meet the needs that keep my table set
Let Your riches answer my arithmetic

verse.text: Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, he gave thanks and broke the loaves. They all ate and were satisfied.

blocks.text: Five loaves, two fish, thousands of people — and the miracle began with giving thanks for the little that was there. God's provision often works that way: He multiplies what you actually have when you thank Him for it. The single parent's 'five loaves' — the small wage, the leftover month-ends, the odd hour — break open in His hands far past what arithmetic allows. Watch for the multiplication, and start with gratitude for the loaves.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Thank God for your current 'loaves and fish'
Offer the small amount, not just the enough
Watch — the feeding often surprises the math

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Multiply the little I have
Feed my household from Your breaking hands

verse.text: Look at the birds of the air; they do not sow or reap… yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they?

blocks.text: Jesus puts birds under your roof to teach the Father's feeding habit: He feeds without sowing, and you are 'much more valuable' than sparrows. The point isn't laziness — birds still work for food — it's freedom: the supply chain is the Father, not your anxiety. When the month looks bare, the verse says look up at a bird and let the 'much more valuable' land on you.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Watch a bird and let the verse sink in
Tell the anxious 'who will feed us' voice the truth
Ask the Father — the birds' feeder — for bread

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Feed me as You feed the birds — and more
Let value, not anxiety, define my supply

verse.text: Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, because God has said, 'Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you.'

blocks.text: The promise that attacks the money-fear is not about cash; it's about presence: Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you. The single parent's deepest fear isn't just a low balance — it's being left, exposed, having no one. God cuts that off with a five-time oath. Contentment with what you have gets possible because the one thing that can't be taken is the promise that won't abandon you.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Stand on the lifetime promise: never forsaken
Let that undercut one money-fear today
Practice contentment from presence, not possessions

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Settle me in the never-forsaken promise
Let Your presence be the provision under provision

verse.text: My God will meet all your needs according to the riches of his glory in Christ Jesus.

blocks.text: Quiz day on provision. One promise to hold against the empty cupboard: meet all your needs. Check what you remember, then trust the Supplier.

blocks.question: According to Philippians 4:19, by what measure does God meet our needs?
options: The riches of his glory in Christ Jesus
blocks.explain: 'My God will meet all your needs according to the riches of his glory in Christ Jesus.' His riches, not ours, set the scale.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Run my provision on Your riches
Meet the need, and settle the fear

verse.text: She went away and did as Elijah had told her. So there was food every day for Elijah and for the woman and her family.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the widow of Zarephath rests fully in the jar's story: she acted on the word, and 'there was food every day.' Every day. Not a lump sum for a season; daily bread, again. Rest is possible when you track provision as a daily pattern instead of a monthly gamble. The God who has fed her and your family through every past day holds today as the next in the pattern.

blocks.prompt: Can you list the daily provisions God has already made in your story? Let the pattern, not the panic, describe your future.
blocks.placeholder: The food that has already appeared...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Show me the pattern of Your daily bread
Rest my month on the rhythm, not the risk

verse.text: Jesus answered, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never go hungry.'

blocks.text: The week ends given the deepest answer to every hunger: Jesus is the bread of life. Beyond rent and groceries, there is a hunger that only He fills and that never returns. The single parent's provision story is a shadow of the deeper way God provides: He gave His Son as bread for the whole household — yours included. Whatever the month holds, the table of the Bread of Life is already set and never runs out.

blocks.prompt: What hunger in you (not in the cupboard) needs to be fed by the Bread of Life this week?
blocks.placeholder: The hunger Jesus is feeding...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Feed me and my children with the Bread of Life
Never let us hunger in the way that matters most

intro.text: Every single parent carries a story of loss — betrayal, abandonment, failure, death. This week is about the strangest strength of all: letting God redeem the former things by not letting them define the new ones.

verse.text: Forget the former things; do not dwell on the past. See, I am doing a new thing!

blocks.text: Israel's story — slavery, wilderness — was their whole identity, and God's command startled them: forget the former things. Not amnesia; redirection. Stop dwelling there, because I am doing a NEW thing. A single parent's past — the failed marriage, the loss, the 'what if' — can be the loudest room in the house. God is redirecting your attention to what He's building, which is not a repeat of what broke.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Write down one 'former thing' you keep dwelling on
Hand it to the God who does new things
Turn your eyes toward the new thing today

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Redeem the former things; don't let them own me
Show me the new thing You are doing

verse.text: Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

blocks.text: The 'former things' include your own failures — the choices, the regrets, the day you melted down with the kids. The deepest anchor verse a single parent can stand on: no condemnation to those in Christ. Not 'some condemnation, but manageable' — NONE. The verdict on your past was already handed down at the cross. If you're still hearing the condemner's voice, it is not coming from the bench.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Catch one self-condemning sentence today
Answer it with Romans 8:1's 'no condemnation'
Let the verdict of Christ settle your past

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Silence the voice that condemns me
Let me live from the 'no condemnation'

verse.text: Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you.

blocks.text: The 'former things' include the people who wronged you. Forgiveness, the verse anchors, is not a feeling; it's an act patterned on how God forgave you. Forgiveness doesn't make the wound imaginary or the person safe to re-enter — it releases you from the debt-collecting that was corroding your own month. The children watch you forgive; that's part of their inheritance. Kind and compassionate — even toward the one who left? The cross says yes.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name one person you're still charging rent to
Release the debt — forgiveness is a transaction, not a feeling
Receive the forgiveness you're extending

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach me to forgive as I have been forgiven
Let forgiving free me more than them

verse.text: Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!

blocks.text: The old has gone — that's not an aspiration, it's a fact for those in Christ. The 'old you' constructed by the past is replaced. The person who failed, the person who was failed — that arrangement is finished in Christ; a new creation is here. This is the verse to read the way a single parent needs it read straight: you are not your history. You are a new creation, and the new thing is now.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Declare over yourself: 'the old has gone'
Stop reintroducing yourself with the old label
Do one thing only the new creation would do

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make me new and keep me new
Let the new creation undercut the old story

verse.text: See, I am doing a new thing!

blocks.text: Quiz day on the former things. One turn to own: from dwelling to new. Check what you remember, then do the turning.

blocks.question: In Isaiah 43:19, what does God urge about the past?
options: Forget the former things — He is doing a new thing
Acknowledge it was all for nothing
blocks.explain: 'Forget the former things; do not dwell on the past. See, I am doing a new thing!' God redirects the gaze—not amnesia but newness.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Redirect my gaze to the new thing
Let the former things serve, not rule

verse.text: He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.

blocks.text: Rest day — and this is the rest the former things will eventually know: every tear wiped, the old order passed away. The grief of the single parent — the empty seat at the table, the missing paycheck of a partner, the long nights alone — all of it is provisional now and terminal then. Let the promise do its work on your shoulders today. The story ends with wiping, not remembering.

blocks.prompt: Which tears do you keep wiping yourself that God has promised to wipe? Sit with the end of the story for a moment.
blocks.placeholder: The tears He will wipe are...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep my hope in the wiping day
Let the last chapter settle this week

verse.text: Neither do people pour new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the skins will burst… rather, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.

blocks.text: The week closes with the strange invitation of the new: the new thing won't fit in the old containers. What God is pouring into this season — your new strength, your new family shape, your new identity — needs whatever is flexible to hold it. Let the rigid parts of your old story soften so the new wine doesn't burst them. The former things taught you; the new wineskins carry what God is pouring now.

blocks.prompt: Which 'old wineskin' in your life needs to make room for what God is pouring now? What would receiving the new thing require you to release?
blocks.placeholder: The old wineskin I'll release is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make me a vessels for the new thing
Preserve both the wine and the one who pours

intro.text: For the child of a single parent, hope can be the rarest gift. This week we strengthen the children's future: what Scripture promises children, and the hope we build into them — not as pressure, but as inheritance.

verse.text: Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him.

blocks.text: In a culture where kids can feel like a problem, Scripture calls them a heritage and a reward — from the Lord. That reframes everything about the single-parent load: the children themselves are the inheritance, given by God. Not a burden you're carrying, but a reward you've been entrusted with. Parenting from that frame clears the guilt and lights the work: these are gifts, not grades.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Look at each child through 'heritage from the Lord'
Say it out loud when the load feels heavy
Treat the gift as a reward, not a debt

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Thank You for these gifts who are my heritage
Let me steward the reward, not resent the load

verse.text: One generation commends your works to another; they tell of your mighty acts.

blocks.text: There is a relay in the psalm: one generation commends God's works to the next. The children don't inherit only your poverty or your pain; they inherit the story — what God has done for your household. Tell them. The 'mighty acts' include the months he fed you, the night He carried you, the anger He cooled. Hope is built by testimony. Generation to generation, the commending is the inheritance.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Tell a child one thing God did for your family
Make it part of the routine — a story at dinner
Let the next generation hold the testimony

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make my testimony their inheritance
Let the relay of Your works never break

verse.text: The Lord is my shepherd, I lack nothing.

blocks.text: The best thing you can build into a child is not armor but a shepherd. The child who learns 'the Lord is my shepherd, I lack nothing' can walk into a world you can't watch — because they carry a Shepherd you've introduced them to. You give provision now; you give a Provider forever. Teach the psalm that carried you; it becomes the staff in their hand.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Walk a child through Psalm 23 in simple words
Let them hear 'I lack nothing' from a parent's faith
Show them the Shepherd you lean on

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be Shepherd to my children after me
Let them lack nothing because they know You

verse.text: But Jesus called the children to him and said, 'Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.'

blocks.text: The single-parent fear is that the hard story means the children missed out. Jesus says the kingdom belongs to children like them — not the guarded, privileged, perfect-started ones. 'Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them.' The hindering Jesus names is our filtering, our worry, our 'they're not ready.' Bring them. The kingdom receives them more readily than any school or family ideal.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Bring a child to Jesus — in prayer, at home, in church
Stop the filtering; let the kingdom do its seeing
Believe their story is exactly the kingdom's type

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Receive my children into Your kingdom
Let no hindering of mine slow them

verse.text: Children are a heritage from the Lord.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the heritage. One frame to keep: the kids are a gift and a hope. Check what you remember, then go bless a child.

blocks.question: How does Psalm 127:3 describe children?
options: A heritage from the Lord, a reward from him
blocks.explain: 'Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him.' From the Lord — the gift frame changes the load.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Crown my children with heritage-hope
Let me raise them as the reward they are

verse.text: 'For I know the plans I have for you,' declares the Lord, 'plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.'

blocks.text: Rest day — and the resting place is your children's future. The plans-to-hope-and-future verse was written to exiles, people whose circumstances suggested otherwise; it holds for every family with 'a future' the world doubts. You don't have to engineer the children's whole future; God already has plans for them. Rest means loosening the grip on outcomes you were never meant to manufacture. The Planner is planning.

blocks.prompt: Which of your children's futures are you trying to engineer rather than trust? What would handing the plans over look like?
blocks.placeholder: I'm handing You the plans for...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Plan my children's hope and future
Let me rest in a Planner, not a worrier

verse.text: He tends his flock like a shepherd: He gathers the lambs in his arms and carries them close to his heart.

blocks.text: The week ends where hope always ends — with the Shepherd and the lambs. Your children are gathered in the arms of the One who carries lambs close to His heart. Yes, your arms are full; so are His. The heritage of hope is that the lambs are never fatherless and never motherless, because the Shepherd holds the flock close. Their hope, and yours, is in the arms that don't tire.

blocks.prompt: What does it change to know your children are already in the Shepherd's arms — carried matter-of-factly, close to His heart?
blocks.placeholder: Because He carries them, I can...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Carry my lambs close to Your heart
Let them know they are gathered, never alone

weeks.title: Week 10 — A seat at two tables

intro.text: If you co-parent, you're learning the hardest act of grace in the modern family: two tables, one child. This week is about stewarding that arrangement with kindness, boundaries and a child-shaped lens — even when the other table isn't easy to love.

verse.text: Therefore, as God's chosen people, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience.

blocks.text: Paul lists a wardrobe and says put it on: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience. Co-parenting is where this wardrobe gets tested the hardest — because the other parent can trigger every old wound. Dressing is daily and deliberate. Kindness is not agreement with a wrong or a surrender of boundaries; it is the garment you wear while holding both. God clothes you with it first.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Choose one 'garment' — kindness, gentleness — for the next exchange
Keep the boundary; lay down the bitterness
Remember you are 'holy and dearly loved' underneath the clothes

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Clothe me in compassion before I speak to them
Guard my side of the table, kind and clear

verse.text: If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.

blocks.text: The phrase 'as far as it depends on you' is the whole wisdom of co-parenting: you can't control the other table's choices, but you can run your side of the peace. Some relationships won't be peaceful no matter what you do — the verse releases you from the impossible part while keeping the possible part. Do what is on your side: calm messages, kept promises, a child kept out of the middle.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Run your side of one conflict well — keep it peaceward
Release the part that doesn't depend on you
Let the child never carry your scoreboard

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let peace, as far as it depends on me, win
Release the other side's part to You

verse.text: Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves.

blocks.text: In co-parenting, humility looks specific: the child's need above my win. 'Value others above yourselves' — the 'other' includes the co-parent when it's about the child. Humility doesn't read as weakness; it's the deliberate choice to let the child's cause trump your score. Today, ask: is this decision really for my child's sake, or for my pride? The humble load carries the child's table without dropping it.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Check one decision: is it child-first or pride-first?
Value the child's seat, not your victory
Let humility outrank the last word

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Give me humility that puts my child first
Let my 'win' be their peace

verse.text: Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.

blocks.text: The hardest verse in co-parenting: bless those who persecute you. It's not about returning to abuse or faking friendship; it's the choice not to feed the cycle with cursing. Blessing the co-parent who makes it hard looks like refusing to badmouth in front of the child, speaking the truth without venom, and praying for their good. The child is watching you bless. That is worth more than any court victory.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Bless — don't curse — the hard person in your life
Keep the child out of grown-up animosity
It's not weakness; it's the harder strength

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach me to bless the one who makes it hard
Let my child see blessing win

verse.text: If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the two tables. One phrase to carry: as far as it depends on you. Check what you remember, then run your table well.

blocks.question: What is the key phrase for peaceful relationships in Romans 12:18?
options: As far as it depends on you, live at peace
blocks.explain: 'If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.' Your assignment is your side of the peace.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let me hold my side of peace well
Release the rest to You

verse.text: Let your gentleness be evident to all. The Lord is near.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the gentleness verse has a quiet logline: 'The Lord is near.' In the tension of co-parenting, the nearness of the Lord is the rest. You don't have to win the battle because He is near the field. Gentleness is possible when you're not panicked. Let the nearness do its calming: you are watched over, seated, and the 'as far as it depends on you' assignment is manageable because He is close.

blocks.prompt: Where in the co-parenting tension are you running on fear instead of the Lord's nearness? What would 'the Lord is near' change about your posture?
blocks.placeholder: The Lord is near, so I can...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let Your nearness do the gentleness
Rest me in the peace You are beside

verse.text: All your children will be taught by the Lord, and great will be their peace.

blocks.text: The week ends with the hope that outlasts every custody arrangement: God teaches the children of the faithful. 'All your children will be taught by the Lord,' and the blessing attached is 'great will be their peace' — a peace not dependent on two perfect tables. Even with divided homes, the children can be taught by the Lord of both tables and carry a peace that outruns the division. That's the redemption you keep praying in.

blocks.prompt: What peace is the Lord teaching your child that no arrangement can split? Thank Him for that particular hope.
blocks.placeholder: The peace the Lord is teaching them...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach my children by Yourself
Give them great peace beyond the divided tables

intro.text: The single parent's hardest hours are often the quiet ones — after the kids sleep, when the house is loud with alone. This week we practice what the saints have always known: worship in the night watches is where the Anchor holds the strongest.

verse.text: On my bed I remember you; I think of you through the watches of the night.

blocks.text: David wrote from a wilderness, but his practice was the night watch: in bed, in the dark hours, making the loneliness into remembering. The watches of the night are real for a single parent — 2am, the empty other side of the bed, the worry loop. The psalm turns that stretch into worship: I remember you; I think of you. The night doesn't have to be empty; it can be a chapel.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Turn tonight's waking hours into remembering
When worry wakes you, turn it into 'I remember You'
Let the night watch become the God watch

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Meet me in the watches of the night
Let remembering You outlast the worry

verse.text: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.

blocks.text: Paul and Silas were in a real prison — beaten, feet in stocks — and at midnight they sang. That's not denial; that's the anchor resisting. Their singing had an audience: 'the other prisoners were listening.' Your night-time worship has listeners too — your kids might hear you singing before sleep, and a household's spiritual atmosphere changes when the parent worships in the dark. Sing at midnight. The roof shakes eventually.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Sing one hymn or song tonight — quietly is fine
Let the kids catch you singing in hard times
Stocks don't stop the midnight song

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Put a song in my mouth at midnight
Let the household hear the praise

verse.text: The Lord is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in him, and he helps me. My heart leaps for joy, and with my song I praise him.

blocks.text: Notice the order: he trusts, God helps, and THEN the heart leaps and the song comes. Song isn't only for good times; it's the after-shock of trusting in a night fight. The Lord is my strength and my shield — for a single parent, that's a two-word job description of God covering the house. Trusting Him, help lands, and the heart's response is a song. Pray it, then sing it.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Claim: Lord, be my strength and shield today
Trust, then let the help produce a song
Let joy follow the trusting, not the circumstances

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be my strength and my shield
Let the song lag behind the trust

verse.text: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble.

blocks.text: Back to week one's verse — because the night piles on the memory of the refuge. 'Ever-present help' — present at 2am, present at the empty table, present in the fear about the school fees AND the fear about the teenager's choices. The refrain of this whole season is the refrain of this verse. When the night is long, go back to the well you started in. Ever-present. Still true at midnight.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Recall the week-one refuge in tonight's hour
Announce: 'ever-present help' into the empty room
Let the refrain steady you now

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Ever-present — be present now
Anchor me in the refrain

verse.text: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the songs. One picture to keep: prison, midnight, praise. Check what you remember, then try one note.

blocks.question: What were Paul and Silas doing at midnight in the prison?
options: Praying and singing hymns to God
blocks.explain: 'About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening.' Praise in the darkest hour.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let my midnight sound like theirs
Praise through the bars

verse.text: I will praise the Lord, who counsels me; even at night my heart instructs me.

blocks.text: Rest day — and the psalmist describes a rest that never quite sleeps: the heart that is taught at night. Even in your sleep, God counsels; even the night is a classroom. There's a difference between lying awake in fear and being 'instructed at night' in trust. As you rest today, let the night's wisdom settle in: the Lord counsels even the exhausted. Your sleep is supervised.

blocks.prompt: What has the night (or a sleepless stretch) been teaching you about God recently? Let it be counsel, not merely exhaustion.
blocks.placeholder: The night has been teaching me...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Counsel me even while I rest
Make my night hours a classroom of trust

verse.text: Weeping may stay for the night, but rejoicing comes in the morning.

blocks.text: The week ends with the night's promise contained: weeping may stay for the night — the word picture is of an overnight guest, not a permanent resident — but rejoicing comes with the morning. The single parent's hardest truth and its hope are both in this one line: the weeping is real, and it is temporary. The morning the psalm means is not just sunrise; it's the day the Anchor holds. Sorrow lodges overnight. Rejoicing has the lease.

blocks.prompt: What 'night' are you in that this verse promises a morning for? Who is the rejoicing waiting for after the weeping's stay?
blocks.placeholder: The morning coming after...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let rejoicing find me in the morning
Give the weeping its visit — but not the lease

intro.text: The single-parent family can feel like a flickering lamp. Jesus puts the lamp on a stand — not hidden. This week we own the light: what your family's story means in the neighborhood, and how you shine without apologizing.

verse.text: You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden.

blocks.text: Jesus doesn't say 'if you become light' or 'when life improves.' He says you ARE the light of the world — present tense, to ordinary mostly-unimpressive disciples. Your household, single-parent or not, is built like a town on a hill: visible whether you like it or not. That visibility isn't a threat; it's the assignment. The neighbors are watching a lamp made to sit on a stand.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Refuse to hide your household's light in shame
Let one good thing be seen — a meal, a pray, a kindness
Believe the visibility is the assignment

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let my family's light be seen
Fill the lamp so it stands on the stand

verse.text: Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a bowl. Instead they put it on its stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house.

blocks.text: The lamp under a bowl is the tragedy of a good life hidden by shame, comparison or fear of judgment. But the natural thing — the lamp's purpose — is the stand. What lights a house isn't an impressive vote; it's a lamp on a stand. Your family has a light shaped by everything you've survived. Don't put the bowl over the story. Let the house your kids and your neighbors share be lit.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Catch one 'bowl' you keep over your family's light
Remove it — let the real story be visible
Give light to everyone in the house today

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Set my lamp on the stand
Let every room in this house be lit

verse.text: Let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.

blocks.text: The purpose clause is precise: the shining is 'that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father.' Not 'that they may praise your parenting' or 'that you may be seen.' The light has an endpoint — glory to the Father. The single parent's good deeds — showing up, working hard, praying with the kids, forgiving the unfair — are the exhibition. When neighbors ask 'how does she do it?', that's the door. The answer is the Father.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Do one good deed visibly, with the Father in view
Let the question 'how?' have an answer
Point the glory, not the spotlight

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Make my light point to You
Let my good deeds end in Your glory

verse.text: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.

blocks.text: The brightest verse about light was written into a dark world: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has NOT overcome it. Not might not; has not. Your family lights a corner of a dark neighborhood exactly because darkness is present. The lamp doesn't scan the room for perfect conditions; it shines. The darkness in the story of single-parent life is real — and it is not the last word.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name the 'darkness' your family has faced
Let the light answer it where you live
Shine today like the darkness has no vote

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let my light hold in the dark
Remind me the darkness has not overcome

verse.text: You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the light. One fact to own: you are the light, and it's not hidden. Check what you remember, then turn the lamp up.

blocks.question: What does Matthew 5:14 say about a town built on a hill?
blocks.explain: 'A town built on a hill cannot be hidden.' Visibility is built-in for the light of the world.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Keep my lamp un-hid
Let the town see the hill

verse.text: The Lord has been my dwelling place throughout all generations.

blocks.text: Rest day — because the light doesn't have to be a performance to be a light. Moses called God 'our dwelling place throughout all generations' — the light of your family isn't your output; it's the dwelling. Even when you rest, the God who has been the dwelling for generations keeps the town visible. You don't shine by straining; the lamp shines by connection to the source. Stay connected, and rest well tonight.

blocks.prompt: How does 'God is my dwelling place' change what it means to rest — versus performing your light? Rest as a dwelling, not a demo.
blocks.placeholder: In His dwelling, rest means...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be my dwelling, generation to generation
Let me rest in the light, not produce it

verse.text: They will be called oaks of righteousness, a planting of the Lord for the display of his splendor.

blocks.text: The week ends with the fullest picture of your household: 'oaks of righteousness, a planting of the Lord — for the display of his splendor.' The single-parent oak isn't the scraggly tree; it's deep-rooted, planted BY THE LORD, and its whole purpose is display — His splendor, not your perfection. Grief turned to garland, despair to praise. You are a planting of the Lord in the visible neighborhood; let the display be glorious when it points to Him.

blocks.prompt: What 'splendor of God' does your family's story display that an easy story never could? Who is meant to see it?
blocks.placeholder: My family displays...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Plant me deep like an oak of righteousness
Let my household display Your splendor

weeks.title: Week 13 — A future and a hope

intro.text: Thirteen weeks of anchoring, and now the season's final truth: the anchor of hope was always pointing at a future. This week we look forward — at your children, your strength, your story — and let the hope be bigger than the horizon.

verse.text: 'For I know the plans I have for you,' declares the Lord, 'plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.'

blocks.text: Written to exiles in Babylon — people whose home was gone and whose future looked confiscated — God revealed the plans He'd had all along: not harm, but a future and a hope. The exile verse is the single parent's verse: the circumstances said 'no future,' and God said otherwise. Whatever your household has been through since the season began, the plans have always been toward hope. You are not the casualty of your story; you're its hope-project.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Say the promise over your household out loud
Point to one sign the future is opening
Let 'hope and a future' outlast the exile-feeling

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Show me the plans You've had all along
Give my family a hope that outruns the season

verse.text: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you pass through the rivers, they will not sweep over you.

blocks.text: Notice the verb: pass THROUGH, not around. God promises to be with you in the crossing, not to reroute the river. The single-parent life has river-crossings — and the comfort is that the waters do not sweep over you because He is with you IN them. The future doesn't mean no more rivers; it means no more solo crossings. Look ahead and see the crossings with the promise pre-stamped on them.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Name the river you're standing at the edge of
Enter it with: 'I will be with you'
Walk the crossing, not around it

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be with me in every future crossing
Let the rivers not sweep us over

verse.text: Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.

blocks.text: Steadiness, when repeated, becomes harvest. 'Do not become weary in doing good' — the proper time comes to those who don't give up. A single parent's good is hard to see in real time: the patient night, the extra conversation, the forgiveness offered again. The verse's whole shape is the season you've lived: steady work, unseen harvest, proper time coming. Don't quit the field in spring — the harvest is the future you hope for.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Do the unrewarded good today on purpose
Believe the proper time is heading toward you
Refuse the give-up that forfeits the harvest

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Renew me in the steady doing of good
Bring the harvest I've been planting

verse.text: Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for him.

blocks.text: The future requires one discipline the busy parent resists most: waiting. 'Be still before the Lord and wait patiently.' Growth happens in soil, underground, without applause — the way trees and children and healed hearts grow. The future you're hoping for is being grown in the waiting. You've been still enough to plant all spring; now wait patiently for the Lord to mature what He's already begun. The quiet isn't empty; it's the grow-house.

blocks.title: Try it today
items: Take a full moment of stillness before the Lord
Wait without the frantic check of progress
Let the grow-house have its season

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Teach me patient waiting
Grow what waits in the quiet

verse.text: Plans to give you hope and a future.

blocks.text: Quiz day on the future. One promise to pack for the weeks after spring: hope and a future. Check what you remember, then walk into it.

blocks.question: To whom did God give the promise of 'hope and a future' plans?
blocks.explain: 'For I know the plans I have for you… plans to give you hope and a future' — spoken to exiles whose future looked confiscated. Exactly where you might find yourself.

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Fulfill the plans of hope over our house
Let me live future-ward

verse.text: We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure.

blocks.text: Rest day — and this is the verse that gives the club its name. Hope is an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. The soul of a single parent needs exactly this: something below the surface that holds so the boat at the surface can rest. Not a hope in circumstances, but hope in the One who anchors. Let the whole season resolve into this rest: you are an Anchor, not because your grip is iron, but because your hope is anchored.

blocks.prompt: Where has this season anchored you? What is the 'firm and secure' thing your soul now rests on?
blocks.placeholder: My soul's anchor is...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Be the anchor my soul rests on
Hold me firm and secure beneath the surface

verse.text: See, I am doing a new thing! Now it springs up; do you not perceive it?

blocks.text: The season's last verse is the lookout: 'See, I am doing a new thing! Now it springs up.' A single parent who has held steady through spring is the one positioned to see it — the new thing already springing: the child you thought was stuck, grown; the strength you thought was spent, renewed; the hope you thought was lost, returned. Perception is the final discipline. Look up. The new thing is springing, and you're the one with eyes to see it.

blocks.prompt: What 'new thing' is already springing up in your household that the worry would make you miss? Name it, and let the season end on it.
blocks.placeholder: The new thing I can see springing up...

blocks.title: Pray it today
items: Let me perceive the new thing You are doing
Die the season with eyes wide, hope high
